newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-CHANG SURVIVES UPSET SCARE POSED BY SPAIN'S VILOCA.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CHANG SURVIVES UPSET SCARE POSED BY SPAIN'S VILOCA.

text.p: Michael Chang survived an upset scare on Thursday at the $289,250 U.S. Men's Clay Court Championships, advancing to the quarter-finals after Juan Albert Viloca served for the match against him.
Viloca, ranked 79th and one of a sudden slew of Spaniards in the top 100, bounced back after a one-sided first set to give Chang a mighty battle before the American prevailed 6-2 6-7 (3-7) 7-5.
Petr Korda of the Czech Republic was not so fortunate and became the only seed to fall in second-round play Thursday.
Korda, seeded third in the tournament, never looked in the match as he went down to unseeded clay court specialist Marcelo Filippini of Uruguay 6-3 6-1.
Fifth-seeded Jason Stoltenberg of Australia advanced to the quarters with a 7-6 (7-3) 6-4 victory over Sweden's unseeded Magnus Norman. Stoltenberg will face Filippini next.
Byron Black, the seventh seed from Zimbabwe, earned a quarter-final match with Chang after defeating Dennis van Scheppingen of the Netherlands 7-6 (8-6) 3-6 6-3.

Chang, who will rise to number two in the world on Monday, controlled the match in the first set with Viloca, but things turned around dramatically after Chang failed to serve out the match at 5-4 in the second set.
Viloca, a versatile groundstroker with a stinging forehand and unpredictable variety, took charge, hitting winners all over the court to take the set to the tiebreaker.
Viloca never let go of the lead in the tiebreaker, winning the decider 7-3 when Chang netted a forehand.
His confidence soaring, the 24-year-old Viloca broke Chang in the opening game of the third set. Chang drew level by breaking for 4-4 but immediately dropped serve to trail 5-4.
But Viloca failed to serve out the match as Chang broke him for 5-5, then lost his spirit as Chang won eight of the next nine points seizing a 7-5 victory when Viloca missed a backhand.

"I felt like I was in control and up a set and 5-3 and the whole match turned around," said Chang of the two hour, 25 minute struggle. "I felt like things were slipping away. From there it was a dogfight. I played off the ropes all of the third set.
"All of the Spaniards are really talented. I don't know what they eat."

Said Viloca, "I had the match won but if you don't win when you have the chance it is difficult. Good players give you one chance to win but they don't give you two chances. I knew I had the chance but I started to play badly."
Viloca said the presence of 14 Spaniards in the top 100, the most of any single nation, is inspiring for all of them.
"Every week a Spanish player is winning a tournament," Viloca said. "We practice together and so you are saying if he is winning then you must win also."
